title: Incremental capacity recovery playbook and automation for GPU exhaustion
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Summary:
This ticket captures the post-incident follow-ups and technical action items to prevent and automate recovery from GPU capacity exhaustion events affecting the hosted API. The incident observed sustained queue buildup, token-level throttling, and failed autoscaler responses during a traffic spike. Root causes include conservative autoscaler cooldown settings, contention in the shared burst pool, and lack of a fast recovery path for preemptible instances.

Goals:
- Define an operational playbook for incremental capacity recovery that can be executed automatically and manually.
- Implement automation to reduce mean time to recover (MTTR) from capacity exhaustion by 50%.
- Add observable signals and safety checks to avoid cascade effects (over-scaling, increased costs, or instability).

Scope / Non-Goals:
- Scope: hosted API GPU clusters, serving runtime hooks (admission, batching), autoscaler tuning, and fallback routing to burst/dedicated pools.
- Non-Goals: long-term capacity increases (this ticket focuses on recovery and automation, not procurement).

Proposed components:
1) Playbook states: DETECT -> SOFT-RECOVERY -> AGGRESSIVE-RECOVERY -> STABILIZE -> REVIEW. Each state has clear metric triggers and runbook steps (manual and automated).
2) Soft-Recovery automation: temporary admission control (reduce req concurrency per-client), raise admission-priority for production OLTP routes, enable prefix-KV cache warming and stake a prebuilt cache snapshot to reduce per-token cost for hot clients.
3) Aggressive-Recovery automation: auto-scale by increasing desired GPU pool by +20% quickly using warm preprovisioned instances, enable preemptible burst if available, and adjust scheduler to favor low-latency work. Include rollback guards (cost cap and latency SLO checks).
4) Circuit breakers: implement per-cluster circuit-breakers to fast-fail new long-running requests when queue depth > X (configurable), with a short retry-after TTL.
5) Observability: new dashboard panels (queue depth by cluster, admission-drop-rate, autoscaler-decision-latency) and alerting rules that map to DETECT state.
6) Test harness and canary: synthetic traffic runner to validate recovery automation on non-prod clusters and a canary flow for gradual rollout to production.

Key metric triggers (initial proposals, subject to tuning):
- DETECT -> queue depth >= 3000 tokens across cluster for 60s OR 95th latency > 1.5x SLO for 30s.
- SOFT-RECOVERY -> queue depth >= 5000 tokens OR admission-drop-rate > 0.5% for 120s.
- AGGRESSIVE-RECOVERY -> sustained queue depth >= 8000 tokens for 3 minutes OR autoscaler desired != actual for > 3 minutes.
- Circuit-breaker firing threshold: per-GPU queue > 400 tokens.

Acceptance criteria:
- Automated soft-recovery lowers queue build-up in synthetic replay tests by >= 40% within 2 minutes.
- Aggressive-recovery automation completes scale-up within target SLA (5 minutes) in canary clusters.
- New dashboard and alerts available in Console and linked to on-call runbook.

Risks / Trade-offs:
- Faster scale-up increases cloud spend during false positives. Mitigation: cost caps and rollback triggers tied to latency metrics.
- Complex admission logic can cause unfair rejections for some customers. Mitigation: priority tiers and explicit per-customer whitelisting.

Next steps / action items (owners):
- A1: Draft the DETECT->STABILIZE state machine and metric thresholds (owner: Rafael) — 2d.
- A2: Prototype soft-recovery admission control and KV cache warming endpoint (owner: Nikhil) — 5d.
- A3: Implement aggressive-recovery autoscaler hook with warm pool provisioning + rollback guard (owner: Priya) — 8d.
- A4: Dashboard panels + alerts + runbook pages in Console/Confluence (owner: Maya) — 3d.
- A5: Build synthetic traffic tester and run canary (owner: SRE team lead: Luca) — 4d.
- A6: Post-rollout incident simulation and SLA cost analysis (owner: PM: Anya) — 3d.

comments: 2026-03-05 Maya Chen: Created ticket after postmortem sync. Initial proposals aggregated from SRE + runtime teams.

2026-03-06 Rafael Ortega: Ran initial load replay on staging; observed autoscaler lag ~4.8m when cold-starting additional GPUs. Noted throttle logic blocks new requests even when capacity is being provisioned.

2026-03-07 Nikhil Gupta: Prototype admission controller implemented — supports per-route priority and temporary concurrency caps. PR opened: runtime#6142. Needs integration tests for fairness across tenants.

2026-03-08 Priya Singh: Designed warm-Pool API for quick provisioning with pre-warmed CUDA contexts. Draft PR autoscaler#229. Cost simulation shows ~12% incremental spend during triggered events; acceptable with cost cap guard.

2026-03-09 Luca Moretti (SRE): Set up synthetic traffic runner and ran three 10-minute canaries on non-prod cluster. Soft-recovery reduced queue depth by 48% in canary 2. Need to tune circuit-breaker thresholds to avoid noisy-failures.

2026-03-10 Anya Rodriguez (PM): Coordinating customer communication template; recommending a throttling transparency banner for highest tiers during rollout. Also requested a playbook review with Solutions Engineers.
2026-03-11 Rafael Ortega: Merged initial runbook to Confluence and scheduled a cross-team demo on 2026-03-12. Next: finish automations and run controlled production canary.
